name: Treaty at Camp Klamath (1851), unratified California treaty Q
aka: Treaty Q of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 3 or 4 set apart a defined tract 'forever' for the occupancy of the signing tribes.
Beef cattle and flour for subsistence during 1851 and 1852.
Livestock, ploughs, tools, seed, iron and steel, blankets and clothing, divided by the tribes' numbers.
A farmer, a blacksmith, a carpenter and school teachers, with a school house, for at least five years.

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty Q in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States Senate, executive session; record reprinted 1905

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

breaches.what: The Karuk Tribe states that because the 1851 treaties were never ratified the reservations they promised were never created, and that the 1905 Klamath Forest Reserve then took its entire aboriginal territory as public land without recognizing Karuk title.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Karuk Tribe, Office of Tribal Lands Management history timeline

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 303, 304 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

nationVoice.summary: The preamble to the Yurok Constitution says that after gold miners overran Yurok land the people agreed to a Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the President's representatives in 1851, that the Senate failed to ratify it, and that the United States then confined the Yurok to an executive order reserve in 1855 and left them only small parts of their land in later reservations.

The Tribe's land office says none of the treaties Redick McKee negotiated in 1851 were ratified, so the reservations they promised were never created, and that in 1905 the Klamath Forest Reserve claimed the whole 1.04 million acre Karuk aboriginal territory as public land, leaving the Tribe without recognized title to its 117 villages; it has since bought back 1,661 acres.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: Hoopa Valley Tribe, California; Klamath Tribes, Oregon.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.

Article 2 of the treaties had the tribes relinquish all their lands in California; because the Senate rejected the treaties, the United States took the land without the reserved tracts or the promised goods (1928 Act, section 2).
